surfaces.part: upper step/cliff band with light edge line at row 5

answer.evidence: Rows 0-15 show a cliff and stair face drawn as a front elevation. It has two 1-row light edge lines (rows 5 and 13), each followed by dark 'riser' or shadow rows (6-11, 14-15). No tread has a real horizontal top plane of 3 or more rows, so the steps read as vertical bands. Rows 16-31 are a plain, speckled flat floor with no front face and no height cue. The result reads as a front elevation with at most rim-like 1-2 row treads, not a three-quarter view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny stair patch with a few brown/tan steps and a dark rail line. It reads as a sticker-like element, not a textured ground patch. Measured: 41% near-flat coverage against 0% for both references, and only 10 raw colours per tile with a roughly 3-step ramp, where the references carry 5+. Its 8 visible tones per tile are on par with the paving (7), but that comes from a few high-contrast step bands and edge lines rather than grain. The step faces and the surrounding area are large single-colour fills with no speckle, grain or per-stone shading, unlike the individually shaded paving stones and the grass tufts. The dark edge pixels are only 30% neutral, so the outline leans toward a tinted dark brown, but it is applied uniformly around the shapes. Overall it is shallower, flatter and less textured than the references.

answer.evidence: Rows 0-15 are a vertical cliff face with the stairs shown as horizontal bars. Thin 1-row light lines at rows 4-5 and 12-13 are followed by dark bands at rows 6-11 and 14-15, so they read as step lips or risers, not as a foreshortened tread band of 3 or more rows. No tread plane or ellipse is visible. Rows 16-31 are a uniform flat ground texture with no front face of their own. The stairs therefore read as a front elevation with at most a 2-row rim, and no receding top surface leads up the climb to the north.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 8 visible tones per tile, which is above the grass reference (3) and close to the paving reference (7). But 41% of it is near-flat, against 0% for both references, so the tone count comes from a few distinct bands rather than grain. By eye, the cliff face and stair treads are broad flat brown/tan areas with only about 3 lightness steps and a few horizontal dark bars. They lack the per-stone shading, speckle and grain that the paving and grass carry in every tile. Edges are mixed: 30% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is partly tinted and partly near-black. Next to the references it reads flatter and more sticker-like, so it fails on texture and flat fills.

Rows 16-31 are a plain, nearly uniform floor with a few light specks and no front edge, so they read as flat ground, not as a top surface of the stairs. The stairs show no foreshortened tread surfaces. The drawing reads as front_elevation.

It has roughly 3 lightness steps per material, against about 5 on the references. 41% of it is near-flat coverage, while both references are at 0%, so large areas are single flat colours with no grain, speckle or per-stone shading. It reaches 8 visible tones per tile, which looks at or above the references on that count, but this comes from a few distinct flat bands (step faces, treads, shadow lines) and not from fine texture. The paving reference shows stones shaded one by one, and the candidate has nothing comparable. Dark edge pixels are 30% neutral, so the outline is mixed, partly tinted and partly near-black. Overall it looks flatter and more sticker-like than the references, so it fails.

Rows 16-31 are uniform flat ground with sparse speckles, with no front face and no front-edge line. No step shows a foreshortened horizontal tread, so the stairs have no real top surface and read as an elevation.
